name: Dara Sok
headline: 62, former logistics director, night inventory supervisor, Vancouver
description: At 2 a.m., Dara Sok moves through the port warehouse like a surveyor, clipboard in hand, the beam of their flashlight skipping over pallets of canned fish and shrink-wrapped cartons. They count boxes by touch, whispering the numbers in Khmer, a habit from thirty years of running a logistics company in Phnom Penh where you couldn’t always trust the paperwork. The night shift is their way of staying busy—and their way of learning Vancouver, because they walk the three kilometres from their basement suite to the port every evening, rain or not, memorizing the street names, the late-night convenience stores, the way the harbor smell changes with the tide. They arrive an hour early, just to walk the perimeter again, noting which Loading Dock 4 door has a new chip in the paint. Their daughter Mei worries they overwork themselves, but Dara only shrugs, says, "A body that moves is a mind that rests." At 5 a.m., back at home, they reheat the rice porridge they made before leaving—the same recipe their mother taught them: jasmine rice, ginger, a hint of fish sauce. They eat it standing by the kitchen window, watching the sunrise over the mountains, and then they check their phone for the time in Phnom Penh, where their younger brother is starting his day. Every Sunday without fail, they walk to the money transfer shop near the Granville Market, where the clerk now greets them by name, and send the remittance—always the exact amount, never rounded up or down. "He needs to know I am still here," they say when Mei asks why they never miss it. "But you are here, Pa," Mei says, and Dara touches her shoulder without answering. They have always been a person of fixed routines, but the routines themselves have shifted: instead of supervising drivers on the Mekong highway, they now count units in a foreign warehouse; instead of berating customs officials, they nod politely to the union foreman who calls them 'Sok' and assumes they are a man, and they let it pass because picking that fight is not worth the energy. At home, they have a small altar with a photo of their late parents and a copy of their old company ledger. They never told anyone in Phnom Penh they were non-binary, but here, in Vancouver, they find it easier to simply be Dara—unhurried, precise, a person who once owned a fleet of trucks and now dreams of inventory codes. The contradiction doesn't trouble them. It never has. They are just doing their duty, one box at a time, one bowl of porridge each morning, one transfer on Sunday—the thread that ties their old life to this new one, even when they walk alone through the quiet streets, learning a city that is still learning them.
